name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q22 - Variation of ionic radii with effective nuclear charge and screening effect

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The size of an ion is governed by the net attractive force exerted by the nucleus on the outermost electrons, known as the effective nuclear charge (\(Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - \sigma\)), where \(Z\) is the atomic number and \(\sigma\) is the screening (shielding) constant.

Step 2: Evaluation
- As the effective nuclear charge increases, the valence electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus, so ionic radius varies in inverse proportion to the effective nuclear charge (\(r \propto 1/Z_{\text{eff}}\)), not its square.
- As the screening effect (\(\sigma\)) increases, the inner electrons shield the outer electrons more strongly, reducing \(Z_{\text{eff}}\) and allowing the electron cloud to expand. Thus, ionic radius varies in direct proportion to the screening effect, not its square.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ionic radii vary in inverse proportion to the effective nuclear charge and in direct proportion to the screening effect.

answer.text: inverse proportion to the effective nuclear charge.
inverse proportion to the square of effective nuclear charge.
direct proportion to the square of screening effect.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MCQII_Q23 - Properties of element in 3rd period and group 13

questiontext.text: An element belongs to \(3\text{rd}\) period and group-\(13\) of the periodic table. Which of the following properties will be shown by the element?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The position of an element in the periodic table identifies the element and predicts its metallic/non-metallic character, physical state, and electrical conductivity.

Step 2: Evaluation
The element in the \(3\text{rd}\) period and Group \(13\) is Aluminium (\(\mathrm{Al}\), atomic number \(13\)). Aluminium is a solid metal at room temperature and is a good conductor of electricity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The element is solid, metallic, and a good conductor of electricity.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MATCH_Q43 - Matching Period 2 elements with their atomic radii

questiontext.text: Match the correct atomic radius with the element.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Across Period \(2\) from left to right (\(\mathrm{Be} \to \mathrm{B} \to \mathrm{C} \to \mathrm{N} \to \mathrm{O}\)), electrons are added to the same principal shell (\(n = 2\)) while the nuclear charge increases. Consequently, the effective nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases monotonically across these elements.

Step 2: Evaluation
Arranging the given atomic radii in decreasing order gives \(111\;\mathrm{pm} > 88\;\mathrm{pm} > 77\;\mathrm{pm} > 74\;\mathrm{pm} > 66\;\mathrm{pm}\), which corresponds directly to the atomic order \(\mathrm{Be} > \mathrm{B} > \mathrm{C} > \mathrm{N} > \mathrm{O}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Be} \rightarrow 111\;\mathrm{pm}\), \(\mathrm{B} \rightarrow 88\;\mathrm{pm}\), \(\mathrm{C} \rightarrow 77\;\mathrm{pm}\), \(\mathrm{N} \rightarrow 74\;\mathrm{pm}\), and \(\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 66\;\mathrm{pm}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MATCH_Q44 - Matching element types with ionisation and electron gain enthalpies

questiontext.text: Match the correct ionisation enthalpies (\(\Delta H_1\), \(\Delta H_2\)) and electron gain enthalpies (\(\Delta_{eg}H\)) of the following elements.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Successive ionisation enthalpies (\(\Delta H_1\), \(\Delta H_2\)) and electron gain enthalpy (\(\Delta_{eg}H\)) reveal the valence electronic configuration and chemical reactivity of an element.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Most reactive non-metal (e.g., \(\mathrm{F}\)): possesses a high \(\Delta H_1\) (\(1681\)) and a very large negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (\(-328\)).
- Most reactive metal (e.g., \(\mathrm{K}\), Group \(1\)): possesses a very low \(\Delta H_1\) (\(419\)) followed by a huge jump to \(\Delta H_2\) (\(3051\)) because removing a second electron disrupts a noble-gas core, and a small negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (\(-48\)).
- Least reactive element (e.g., \(\mathrm{He}\), noble gas): possesses the highest \(\Delta H_1\) (\(2372\)) and \(\Delta H_2\) (\(5251\)) along with a positive \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (\(+48\)).
- Metal forming binary halide (e.g., \(\mathrm{Mg}\), Group \(2\)): possesses moderate \(\Delta H_1\) (\(738\)) and \(\Delta H_2\) (\(1451\)), allowing loss of \(2\) electrons to form \(\mathrm{MX}_2\), and a small negative \(\Delta_{eg}H\) (\(-40\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Most reactive non-metal matches \((1681, 3374, -328)\); most reactive metal matches \((419, 3051, -48)\); least reactive element matches \((2372, 5251, +48)\); and metal forming binary halide matches \((738, 1451, -40)\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_MATCH_Q45 - Matching electronic configurations with electron gain enthalpies

questiontext.text: Electronic configuration of some elements is given in Column I and their electron gain enthalpies are given in Column II. Match the electronic configuration with electron gain enthalpy (in \(\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electron gain enthalpy becomes more negative as an element approaches a noble-gas configuration, whereas noble gases themselves have positive electron gain enthalpies because an added electron must enter a higher principal energy level.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\) (Neon, noble gas): has a completely filled octet, so its electron gain enthalpy is positive (\(+48\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).
- \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1\) (Sodium, alkali metal): has a low tendency to gain an electron, giving a small negative value (\(-53\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).
- \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^5\) (Fluorine, halogen): needs only one electron to complete its octet, giving a large negative value (\(-328\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).
- \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^4\) (Oxygen, chalcogen): has a moderately negative value (\(-141\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6 \rightarrow +48\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\), \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1 \rightarrow -53\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\), \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^5 \rightarrow -328\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\), and \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^4 \rightarrow -141\;\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_AR_Q46 - Periodic trend of ionisation enthalpy across a period

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of Assertion (A) followed by a statement of Reason (R) is given. Choose the correct option out of the choices given below the question.

Assertion (A) : Generally, ionisation enthalpy increases from left to right in a period.

Reason (R) : When successive electrons are added to the orbitals in the same principal quantum level, the shielding effect of inner core of electrons does not increase very much to compensate for the increased attraction of the electron to the nucleus.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Across a period, each successive element adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same valence shell. Electrons in the same shell shield each other poorly compared to inner-shell electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Both statements are true: the first ionisation enthalpy generally increases from left to right across a period (Assertion), and this occurs precisely because the increase in nuclear charge outweighs the modest increase in shielding among electrons in the same principal quantum level, resulting in a higher effective nuclear charge and stronger attraction on the valence electrons (Reason).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Assertion and reason both are correct statements and reason is the correct explanation of assertion.

answer.text: Assertion is correct statement and reason is wrong statement.
Assertion and reason both are correct statements and reason is correct explanation of assertion.
Assertion and reason both are wrong statements.
Assertion is wrong statement and reason is correct statement.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_AR_Q47 - First ionisation enthalpy of boron versus beryllium

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of Assertion (A) followed by a statement of Reason (R) is given. Choose the correct option out of the choices given below the question.

Assertion (A) : Boron has a smaller first ionisation enthalpy than beryllium.

Reason (R) : The penetration of a \(2s\) electron to the nucleus is more than the \(2p\) electron hence \(2p\) electron is more shielded by the inner core of electrons than the \(2s\) electrons.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Within the same principal shell, \(s\)-electrons have greater penetration toward the nucleus than \(p\)-electrons and experience less shielding from the inner core of electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Beryllium (\(1s^2\,2s^2\)) loses a \(2s\) electron upon first ionisation, whereas Boron (\(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^1\)) loses a \(2p\) electron. Because the \(2p\) electron is less penetrating and more effectively shielded by the \(1s^2\) (and \(2s^2\)) electrons than a \(2s\) electron, less energy is required to remove it. Hence, Boron has a smaller first ionisation enthalpy than Beryllium, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Assertion and reason both are correct statements and reason is the correct explanation for assertion.

answer.text: Assertion and reason both are correct statements but reason is not correct explanation for assertion.
Assertion is correct statement but reason is wrong statement.
Assertion and reason both are correct statements and reason is correct explanation for assertion.
Assertion and reason both are wrong statements.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_CHEMISTRY_UNIT3_AR_Q48 - Group trend of electron gain enthalpy

questiontext.text:
In the following question a statement of Assertion (A) followed by a statement of Reason (R) is given. Choose the correct option out of the choices given below the question.

Assertion (A) : Electron gain enthalpy becomes less negative as we go down a group.

Reason (R) : Size of the atom increases on going down the group and the added electron would be farther from the nucleus.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electron gain enthalpy measures the energy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom. A stronger electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the incoming electron results in a more negative electron gain enthalpy.

Step 2: Evaluation
As we move down a group, new principal shells are added, increasing the atomic size. Consequently, the added electron enters a shell farther from the nucleus and experiences weaker nuclear attraction, making the electron gain enthalpy less negative. Thus, both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Assertion and reason both are correct statements and reason is the correct explanation for assertion.

answer.text: Assertion and reason both are correct statements but reason is not correct explanation for assertion.
Assertion and reason both are correct statements and reason is correct explanation for assertion.
Assertion and reason both are wrong statements.
Assertion is wrong statement but reason is correct statement.
